title: Intravital timelapse
summary: A time-lapse of cells moving in tissue, e.g. T cells in a lymph node.
text:
# Recipe: Intravital timelapse

When this is you: A time-lapse of cells moving in tissue, e.g. T cells in a lymph node.

## Steps

1. Drift correct a time series (guide `drift-correct`): Tissue drift would read as movement in every track — remove it before anything else.
2. Segment an image (guide `segment-an-image`): Cellpose finds the cells in most movies — start here.
3. Train a flow model (guide `train-flow-model`) — optional: Only if cellpose misses dim cells: a flow model reads movement instead of brightness.
4. Segment a movie by motion (guide `segment-by-motion`) — optional: With that model: on one dim movie, 0 of the 65 cells cellpose found passed QC.
5. Create and gate populations (guide `gate-populations`): QC before tracking: gate out debris and doublets on size × intensity, then track the gate.
6. Track cells (guide `track-cells`): The composite, so tracks arrive measured — bare tracking leaves every later page empty.
7. Classify behaviour states (guide `behaviour-states`): States per timepoint from speed and angle, plus the transitions between them in each track.
8. Cluster tracks into behaviours (guide `cluster-tracks`): Leiden on whole-track measures plus HMM states and transitions: finer than track averages.

---

# Drift correct a time series

Register a drifting time series so cells stay put between frames.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing; a time series (more than one frame).
Runs: `cleanupImages.driftCorrect`.

1. **Cleanup** — Cleanup holds the corrections you apply before segmenting — drift, autofluorescence, noise.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Only time series are worth correcting — a single frame cannot drift.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Drift correction" from the dropdown.
   - Drift correction on its own — this is the whole operation, not half of one.
   - "AF + drift correction" also removes autofluorescence, if you need that in the same pass.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Drift reference channel — pick a stable, bright structure, not a motile cell.
   - Estimator — multi-lag compares non-adjacent frames, so one bad frame cannot offset the rest.
   - Max frame gap — higher is more robust and slower.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **It made a new version** — Corrections never overwrite your import — they add a version and make it active.
   - Everything downstream reads the ACTIVE version.
   - The row's info icon lists every version the image has.
9. **Did it work?** — Cecelia measures the leftover drift itself and flags it here — hover for the findings.
   - A flag means the reference channel probably lost tracking.
   - Re-run with a clearer, structural channel.

---

# Segment an image

Turn fluorescence into per-cell labels — the entry point for everything else.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing.
Runs: `segment.cellposeMeasure`.

1. **Segment** — Segmentation is the entry point: gating, tracking and clustering all read its output.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Tick as many as you like — one task is queued per image.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Cellpose segment + measure" from the dropdown.
   - Plain "Cellpose segmentation" makes labels only — no measures to gate or cluster on.
   - This one measures too, so everything downstream has something to read.
   - Cells too dim for cellpose in a movie? Segment by motion instead.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Cell channels — the channels carrying the cell signal; they are merged by maximum.
   - Cell diameter (µm) — the single setting that most decides whether this works.
   - Nucleus channels — pair a "nuc" model with a "base" one for nucleus-anchored cells.
   - Clear border cells — drops cells cut off by the image edge.
6. **Preview before you commit** — This runs the real compute over just the region the viewer is showing.
   - Seconds instead of minutes — the way to judge the diameter and channels.
   - Open the image in the viewer first; the preview follows what it shows.
7. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
8. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
9. **Check the QC first** — These plots flag the usual failures — too few cells, implausible sizes, edge artefacts.
   - One population per segmentation, so two runs plot side by side.
   - A weird size distribution almost always means the diameter was off.
10. **Open it in the viewer** — The ↗ opens the image itself — the overlay is a separate switch.
11. **Open the Viewer panel** — This panel drives the viewer — overlays, contrast, 3D, recording.
12. **Switch the mask on** — Nothing is drawn on the image until you toggle the mask for that segmentation.
   - One row per segmentation, each with its own switches.
   - The choice is remembered, so it comes back next time you open the image.
13. **Now judge the mask** — With it on screen, this is what to look for.
   - Are single cells one label, or is a clump merged into one?
   - Are the outlines on the cells, or offset from them?
14. **What you now have** — Labels are in, and measured — which is what makes them useful.
   - Each cell has an id, a centroid and its regionprops + intensity measures.
   - Gate on those next, or track them if this is a time series.

---

# Train a flow model

Teach a model what moving cells look like in your own movies — the step before motion segmentation.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing; a time series (more than one frame).
Runs: `opticalFlow.train`.

1. **Model training** — Motion segmentation learns from movement, so it needs a model trained on movies like yours.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Tick as many as you like — one task is queued per image.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Train flow model" from the dropdown.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Model name — the vault entry this writes; you pick it again when you segment.
   - Channels — the ones showing cell bodies move; the model reads motion, not markers.
   - Max frames per movie — cap it for a first pass, then retrain on more.
   - Epochs — 30 to start; the loss curve says whether it needed more.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **Read the training curves** — This is how you tell a model that learned from one that stalled.
   - A loss still falling at the last epoch means train again with more.
   - Flow metrics show what the model was actually fed.
9. **What you now have** — A model in the vault, not in this project — the same one segments any movie of this kind.
   - Segment with it next, on the Segment page.

---

# Segment a movie by motion

Find cells by how they move rather than how bright they are — for dim, moving cells in tissue.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing; a time series (more than one frame).
Runs: `segment.coastalMeasure`.

1. **Segment** — This segments by motion, so it works where a cell is too dim to find in any single frame.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Tick as many as you like — one task is queued per image.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Optical flow segment + measure" from the dropdown.
   - Needs a trained flow model — run "Train a flow model" first.
   - Plain "Optical flow segmentation" makes labels only, with no measures to gate on.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Model — the one you trained; its manifest fixes the metrics and scales used.
   - Cell channels — the same channels the model was trained on.
   - Seed window (µm) — about one cell across; it decides what counts as one object.
   - Foreground threshold — raise it if background is coming through as cells.
6. **Preview before you commit** — This runs the real compute over just the region the viewer is showing.
   - Seconds instead of minutes — the way to judge the diameter and channels.
   - Open the image in the viewer first; the preview follows what it shows.
7. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
8. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
9. **Check the QC first** — Same plots as any segmentation — too few cells, implausible sizes, edge artefacts.
   - Compare it against a cellpose run on the same image if you have one.
10. **Open it in the viewer** — The ↗ opens the image itself — the overlay is a separate switch.
11. **Open the Viewer panel** — This panel drives the viewer — overlays, contrast, 3D, recording.
12. **Switch the mask on** — Nothing is drawn on the image until you toggle the mask for that segmentation.
   - One row per segmentation, each with its own switches.
   - The choice is remembered, so it comes back next time you open the image.
13. **Now judge the mask** — With it on screen, this is what to look for.
   - Do the labels stay on the same cell as it moves?
   - Is a moving cell one object, or does it break up between frames?
14. **What you now have** — Labels and measures on a movie cellpose could not read — track them next.
   - Tracking is the point of segmenting a movie; gating works on these too.

---

# Create and gate populations

Draw gates on two measures at a time to carve your cells into named populations.

Needs: an open project; a segmented image.

1. **Gate** — Gating is FlowJo-style: pick two measures, draw round the cells you want, name them.
2. **One image at a time** — Gating works on a single image — pick one and its cells load below.
   - Gates can be copied to the rest of the set once you are happy with them.
3. **Which segmentation** — You gate on the measures of one label set — pick it here if you have several.
4. Add a plot — each one is a pair of measures you can draw on.
5. **Choose the two measures** — X and Y take any channel intensity or shape measure the segmentation carried.
   - The transform beside each axis is usually what makes a blob resolve into groups.
   - "pop" is the population you are looking at — new gates land under it.
6. **Pick a shape** — Choose a gate shape, then draw on the plot — drag for a rectangle, click to place polygon points.
   - Hold Shift to adjust a gate you already drew.
7. **Name it** — A population is just a named gate — the name is how everything downstream refers to it.
   - Names are case-insensitively unique across the whole tree, not just among siblings.
   - A leading underscore is reserved for tracked / clustering populations.
8. The population manager shows the tree you are building.
9. **Gates nest** — Each population shows its cell count and its share of its parent.
   - Click one to plot it, then draw inside it to subset further.
   - That nesting is the gating strategy — CD3+ → CD4+ → activated.
10. **Populations are live** — Gates are stored as definitions, not as a frozen list of cells.
   - Re-segment and your gates still apply.
   - Populations show up in the viewer, in plots, and as a tracking input.

---

# Track cells

Link segmented cells across frames into tracks, with speed and direction for free.

Needs: an open project; a time series (more than one frame); a segmented image.
Runs: `tracking.bayesian_track_measures`.

1. **Track** — Tracking links labels across frames — so segment every timepoint before you come here.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Each image needs a segmentation covering all of its frames.
   - It must be a MEASURED segmentation — the Segment guide's function does both.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Bayesian track + measures" from the dropdown.
   - Plain "Bayesian tracking" links cells but computes no per-track measures.
   - This one measures too — speed, displacement, angle — which is what you gate and cluster on.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Segmentation — which label set to track; a gated population narrows it.
   - Max search radius (µm) — the furthest a cell may move between frames (~20 for T cells).
   - Allowed gaps and minimum timepoints — how forgiving linking is, and what counts as a real track.
   - Motion dimensions — 2D or 3D for the measures; it detects and recommends one.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **Open it in the viewer** — The ↗ opens the image itself — the overlay is a separate switch.
9. **Open the Viewer panel** — This panel drives the viewer — overlays, contrast, 3D, recording.
10. **Switch the tracks on** — Nothing is drawn on the image until you toggle the tracks for that segmentation.
   - One row per segmentation, each with its own switches.
   - The choice is remembered, so it comes back next time you open the image.
11. **Now judge the tracks** — With it on screen, this is what to look for.
   - Do the trails follow single cells, or jump between neighbours?
   - Jumping usually means the search radius is too generous.
12. **Gate on track properties** — This is the gating canvas in track mode — one point per track, not per cell.
   - Gate on speed, displacement and the other per-track aggregates.
   - Select exactly one image to use it.
13. **What you now have** — Tracks are in, and measured — speed, displacement and angle came with them.
   - Every cell has a track_id and a position at each timepoint.
   - Behaviour → HMM fits states to those measures; Cluster tracks groups on both.

---

# Classify behaviour states

Fit an HMM to track movement so each cell gets an arrested / directed / meandering state.

Needs: an open project; a tracked image.
Runs: `behaviour.hmm`.

1. **Behaviour** — A Gaussian HMM turns raw track movement into a small set of named behaviour states.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Only tracked images qualify — the states are fitted to track measures.
   - The tracking must have MEASURED — the Track guide's function does both.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "HMM (states + transitions)" from the dropdown.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Number of states — 3 is the usual starting point (arrested / meandering / directed).
   - Which track measures to fit on — speed and angle are the standard pair.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **Read the states off the plots** — The panel shows what each fitted state actually looks like, so you can name them.
   - A state is only meaningful once you have seen its speed profile.
   - Fit landed oddly? Change the number of states and re-run.
9. **Colour tracks by state** — The Viewer panel can colour tracks by the new state column.
   - That is the quickest sanity check that the states mean something.

---

# Cluster tracks into behaviours

Group whole tracks by how they move, rather than grouping cells by what they express.

Needs: an open project; a tracked image.
Runs: `clustTracks.cluster`.

1. **Cluster tracks** — One row per track instead of per cell — so this needs tracking, not just segmentation.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Select every image to cluster TOGETHER — the run pools across them.
   - Needs measured tracks — the Track guide's function does both.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Cluster tracks" from the dropdown.
   - Cell measures are aggregated per track for you; HMM states become per-track frequencies.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Track populations — which tracks to cluster; every selection is clustered jointly.
   - Cluster on — whole-track measures plus the HMM state and transitions columns (run HMM first).
   - Minimum track length — drop tracks too short to characterise.
   - Resolution — the Leiden resolution; higher gives more, smaller clusters.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **Clusters of movement** — The UMAP separates behaviours; the heatmap says which measures define each one.
   - This answers "how many kinds of movement are in here", without naming them first.
   - With the HMM states and transitions in, it separates behaviours track averages blur.
9. **Clusters are numbers, not populations yet** — Open the population manager — this is where numbered clusters become named groups.
10. **Add a population** — There is no gate to draw here — you create the population first, then fill it.
   - Name it for what it is: "patrolling", "CD4 T cell".
11. **Tick clusters into it** — Each chip is one cluster — click to put it in this population.
   - A cluster belongs to at most one population; ticking it elsewhere moves it.
   - The heatmap is how you decide which clusters belong together.
12. **Now it behaves like any population** — Your behaviour populations are usable everywhere a gated one is.
   - Plot them on the analysis board, show them in the viewer, use them as an input.
   - Populations are per clustering run — they follow that run's suffix.

title: Find your way around
summary: The buttons that are not on any page: menu, guides, connection, console, Settings.
text:
# Find your way around

The buttons that are not on any page: menu, guides, connection, console, Settings.


1. **The menu** — Every analysis step is a page in this menu, ordered the way a project runs.
   - Data first, then populations, then analysis.
   - Collapse it when you want the width.
2. **Your project** — Open, create and switch projects here — everything else on screen belongs to this one.
3. **What's new** — The feijoa opens release notes and the tip cards you just came from.
   - Cycle the sketches to see what Cecelia does.
4. **The guides** — This compass lists every guide, including this one — it is how you get back here.
   - Each one walks you through a real step on your own data.
   - A guide only points and watches; it never clicks for you.
5. **Bugs and questions** — GitHub for anything broken, the Zulip chat for anything you are unsure about.
   - Both open outside Cecelia, in a new tab.
   - Questions in chat are welcome — no issue needed.
6. **The backend** — Cecelia is a browser front end onto a Julia server — this says whether it is reachable.
   - Green: connected, and tasks will run.
   - Anything else: the server is down, and nothing will start.
7. **The console** — Warnings and errors land here, newest last, whichever page you were on.
   - Click a line to expand the detail.
   - Worth opening first when something did not happen.
8. **The viewer** — Opens images in the viewer, with segmentations and tracks as layers you can toggle.
9. **The correction cockpit** — Join, split or remove tracks, and edit labels — the hand-tools for fixing what an automated run got wrong.
10. **The lab log** — A per-project record of what was run and what you concluded, kept as you go.
11. **Kiwi — the assist cockpit** — Pairing, chat handoff and the buttons that share what is on screen with Claude — all here.
   - On-demand only: nothing happens until you ask.
12. **Settings** — Two things worth knowing live in here — click through and I will point them out.
13. **Updates** — Your version, and a Check button — a new release installs from here.
   - A shared installation is updated by whoever administers it.
14. **Disk space** — Scan shows where the project’s bytes went, and what can be freed without losing work.
   - Corrections and crops keep the old version around — those are the reclaimable ones.
   - Freeing them keeps each image’s active version.
   - Worth a look before a big run.
15. **Leaving** — Closing the browser tab does not stop Cecelia — the backend keeps running until you quit here.
   - Not now — this is for when you are done for the day.
   - It stops the viewer and the notebook server too.

title: Use a user profile
summary: Who is driving this box — and where switching, creating or logging in a profile lives.
text:
# Use a user profile

Who is driving this box — and where switching, creating or logging in a profile lives.


1. **Who is driving** — The chip in the header names the active profile — click it to open Preferences → Profiles.
   - One profile per person, not per experiment.
2. **The Profiles pane** — Every profile has its own Kiwi credentials, preferences and project list — switching one over reloads the app.
   - No cross-profile sharing by default.
3. **Add a profile** — New profile = fresh credentials and an empty project list.
   - Retire one from the row above; the record stays resolvable for old turn logs.
4. **Log the profile in** — Copies a terminal one-liner scoped to this profile's CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR — paste and run /login.
   - Each profile logs Claude in separately.

title: Use a view profile
summary: Curate the sidebar down to the pages you actually work on — declutter, not access control.
text:
# Use a view profile

Curate the sidebar down to the pages you actually work on — declutter, not access control.


1. **Settings** — View profiles live in Settings — they curate the sidebar down to the pages this user actually works on.
   - This is decluttering, not access control — every page still opens by URL.
2. **Pick or edit one** — The chip row picks which profile is active; Edit opens the builder.
   - "All pages" is the default — you never lose access to a page by picking a profile.
3. **Tick pages into a profile** — One row per sidebar group — tick the pages this profile should surface.
   - Great for handing a colleague a "just the segmentation bits" cecelia.

title: Import images
summary: Register microscopy files and convert them to OME-Zarr, ready to analyse.
text:
# Import images

Register microscopy files and convert them to OME-Zarr, ready to analyse.

Needs: an open project.
Runs: `importImages.omezarr`.

1. **Everything lives in a project** — A project holds your images and every result derived from them.
   - Use the ⋯ menu here to switch projects or make a new one.
2. **Manage images** — Adding, moving and deleting images all happen on this one page.
3. **Pick a set first** — A set groups images you want to treat together — a condition, a day, an experiment.
   - Every function runs against the active set.
4. **Add images** — Browse to your microscopy files — CZI, LIF, ND2, OME-TIFF and friends.
5. **Choose the files** — Tick the images you want; unsupported file types are greyed out.
   - This header checkbox takes every image in the folder at once.
6. Add them to the set.
7. **Added, but not converted yet** — Adding files registers a row per image — it does not read the pixels.
   - Nothing downstream can use an image until it is converted.
   - The eye on the left of each row stays disabled until then.
8. **Tick what to convert** — Select the images you just added — one conversion is queued per image.
   - The flag icon in the Name header selects everything that needs attention.
9. **Choose the function** — Pick "Convert to OME-ZARR" from the dropdown.
10. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Pyramid levels — downscaled copies for fast zoomed-out viewing; 2-3 suits a 512-1024 px frame.
   - Copy to local scratch first — much faster when the source is on a network share.
   - The defaults are right for most files; you can leave Advanced alone.
11. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
12. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
13. **Converted** — The image now has an OME-Zarr, which is what everything downstream reads.
   - The eye is enabled once an image has one.
   - Big time series take a while — you can keep working while they run.
   - Nothing appeared? The run's log in the task rail says why.
14. **Check it opened correctly** — The ↗ opens the image in the viewer — worth doing once per new file type.
   - It stays disabled until that image has converted.
   - Wrong channel count or pixel size means the metadata needs a look.
15. **Ready** — That is import done — your set is ready to clean up or segment.
   - Odd pixel sizes or channel names? Metadata page.
   - Drifting time series? Cleanup page.
   - Otherwise go straight to Segment.

title: Fix pixel size and channel names
summary: Correct the voxel size, frame interval and channel names an import guessed wrong.
text:
# Fix pixel size and channel names

Correct the voxel size, frame interval and channel names an import guessed wrong.

Needs: an open project; at least one image in the current set.

1. **Metadata** — Wrong pixel size silently corrupts every µm measurement downstream — fix it here first.
   - Cell diameters, areas, speeds and distances all depend on it.
2. **Cecelia flags the suspects** — A flag on a row means a metadata field looks implausible — hover to see which.
   - Missing Z spacing and a 1-pixel-per-µm default are the usual two.
3. **Voxel size and timing** — Open the editor to set the real pixel size, Z spacing and frame interval.
   - Select several images to fix them in one pass.
   - Values come from your acquisition software, not from guesswork.
4. **Name the channels** — Real names make every downstream picker readable — "CD4", not "mean_intensity_2".
   - One name per line, in channel order.
   - Copy from a reference image to do a whole set at once.
5. **Add your experimental groups** — Attributes are your own columns — treatment, genotype, mouse, timepoint.
   - They are what plots group and compare by later.
   - Fill them from the filename with the pattern builder.
6. **Do this before you segment** — Metadata is read at run time, so fixing it later means re-running what you already ran.

title: Preprocess an image
summary: Crop / project / resample raw images before you segment — writes a new version, keeps the original.
text:
# Preprocess an image

Crop / project / resample raw images before you segment — writes a new version, keeps the original.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing.
Runs: `editImages.cropImage`.

1. **Preprocessing** — Preprocess sits between import and cleanup — trim the region before every downstream step reads the full one.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Tick as many as you like — one task is queued per image.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Crop image" from the dropdown.
   - Crop is what this guide walks; MIP, bin, resample and dtype sit beside it in the same dropdown.
   - Every preprocess writes a NEW image version — nothing overwrites your import.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Source image — which version of this image to crop; defaults to the active one.
   - Crop area — draw a box on the preview; z/t unset = keep the whole axis.
6. **Preview before you commit** — This runs the real compute over just the region the viewer is showing.
   - Seconds instead of minutes — the way to judge the diameter and channels.
   - Open the image in the viewer first; the preview follows what it shows.
7. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
8. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
9. **It made a new version** — The row picks up an extra version — the info icon lists every version this image has.
   - Everything downstream reads the ACTIVE version.
   - Nothing is destroyed — flip back by making the original active.

title: Drift correct a time series
summary: Register a drifting time series so cells stay put between frames.
text:
# Drift correct a time series

Register a drifting time series so cells stay put between frames.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing; a time series (more than one frame).
Runs: `cleanupImages.driftCorrect`.

1. **Cleanup** — Cleanup holds the corrections you apply before segmenting — drift, autofluorescence, noise.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Only time series are worth correcting — a single frame cannot drift.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Drift correction" from the dropdown.
   - Drift correction on its own — this is the whole operation, not half of one.
   - "AF + drift correction" also removes autofluorescence, if you need that in the same pass.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Drift reference channel — pick a stable, bright structure, not a motile cell.
   - Estimator — multi-lag compares non-adjacent frames, so one bad frame cannot offset the rest.
   - Max frame gap — higher is more robust and slower.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **It made a new version** — Corrections never overwrite your import — they add a version and make it active.
   - Everything downstream reads the ACTIVE version.
   - The row's info icon lists every version the image has.
9. **Did it work?** — Cecelia measures the leftover drift itself and flags it here — hover for the findings.
   - A flag means the reference channel probably lost tracking.
   - Re-run with a clearer, structural channel.

title: Segment an image
summary: Turn fluorescence into per-cell labels — the entry point for everything else.
text:
# Segment an image

Turn fluorescence into per-cell labels — the entry point for everything else.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing.
Runs: `segment.cellposeMeasure`.

1. **Segment** — Segmentation is the entry point: gating, tracking and clustering all read its output.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Tick as many as you like — one task is queued per image.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Cellpose segment + measure" from the dropdown.
   - Plain "Cellpose segmentation" makes labels only — no measures to gate or cluster on.
   - This one measures too, so everything downstream has something to read.
   - Cells too dim for cellpose in a movie? Segment by motion instead.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Cell channels — the channels carrying the cell signal; they are merged by maximum.
   - Cell diameter (µm) — the single setting that most decides whether this works.
   - Nucleus channels — pair a "nuc" model with a "base" one for nucleus-anchored cells.
   - Clear border cells — drops cells cut off by the image edge.
6. **Preview before you commit** — This runs the real compute over just the region the viewer is showing.
   - Seconds instead of minutes — the way to judge the diameter and channels.
   - Open the image in the viewer first; the preview follows what it shows.
7. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
8. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
9. **Check the QC first** — These plots flag the usual failures — too few cells, implausible sizes, edge artefacts.
   - One population per segmentation, so two runs plot side by side.
   - A weird size distribution almost always means the diameter was off.
10. **Open it in the viewer** — The ↗ opens the image itself — the overlay is a separate switch.
11. **Open the Viewer panel** — This panel drives the viewer — overlays, contrast, 3D, recording.
12. **Switch the mask on** — Nothing is drawn on the image until you toggle the mask for that segmentation.
   - One row per segmentation, each with its own switches.
   - The choice is remembered, so it comes back next time you open the image.
13. **Now judge the mask** — With it on screen, this is what to look for.
   - Are single cells one label, or is a clump merged into one?
   - Are the outlines on the cells, or offset from them?
14. **What you now have** — Labels are in, and measured — which is what makes them useful.
   - Each cell has an id, a centroid and its regionprops + intensity measures.
   - Gate on those next, or track them if this is a time series.

title: Train a denoise model
summary: Teach a SUPPORT model your noise floor so weaker frames become readable — the step before segmenting dim movies.
text:
# Train a denoise model

Teach a SUPPORT model your noise floor so weaker frames become readable — the step before segmenting dim movies.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing; a time series (more than one frame).
Runs: `opticalFlow.trainSupportDenoise`.

1. **Model training** — SUPPORT learns your movie's noise by comparing the same pixel across frames — so run drift correction first.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Tick as many as you like — one task is queued per image.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Train denoise model (SUPPORT)" from the dropdown.
   - Run drift correction before this; SUPPORT needs the same pixel to stay put across frames.
   - One model per set — pool the channels you want denoised into a single run.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Model name — the vault entry this writes; you pick it again when you segment or denoise.
   - Channels — pool the ones with the same noise character; one model covers them all.
   - Model size and temporal window — Medium and 61 frames are safe defaults; keep the window odd.
   - Epochs — 20 to start; the loss curve says whether it needed more.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **Read the training curves** — Same read as any training run — a loss still falling means feed it more.
   - A stalled curve early on usually means the input was already clean, not that the model failed.
9. **What you now have** — A denoise model in the vault, not this project — it applies to any movie of this kind.
   - Denoise or segment with it next; the vault list holds it under the name you gave.

title: Train a flow model
summary: Teach a model what moving cells look like in your own movies — the step before motion segmentation.
text:
# Train a flow model

Teach a model what moving cells look like in your own movies — the step before motion segmentation.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing; a time series (more than one frame).
Runs: `opticalFlow.train`.

1. **Model training** — Motion segmentation learns from movement, so it needs a model trained on movies like yours.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Tick as many as you like — one task is queued per image.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Train flow model" from the dropdown.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Model name — the vault entry this writes; you pick it again when you segment.
   - Channels — the ones showing cell bodies move; the model reads motion, not markers.
   - Max frames per movie — cap it for a first pass, then retrain on more.
   - Epochs — 30 to start; the loss curve says whether it needed more.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **Read the training curves** — This is how you tell a model that learned from one that stalled.
   - A loss still falling at the last epoch means train again with more.
   - Flow metrics show what the model was actually fed.
9. **What you now have** — A model in the vault, not in this project — the same one segments any movie of this kind.
   - Segment with it next, on the Segment page.

title: Segment a movie by motion
summary: Find cells by how they move rather than how bright they are — for dim, moving cells in tissue.
text:
# Segment a movie by motion

Find cells by how they move rather than how bright they are — for dim, moving cells in tissue.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing; a time series (more than one frame).
Runs: `segment.coastalMeasure`.

1. **Segment** — This segments by motion, so it works where a cell is too dim to find in any single frame.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Tick as many as you like — one task is queued per image.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Optical flow segment + measure" from the dropdown.
   - Needs a trained flow model — run "Train a flow model" first.
   - Plain "Optical flow segmentation" makes labels only, with no measures to gate on.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Model — the one you trained; its manifest fixes the metrics and scales used.
   - Cell channels — the same channels the model was trained on.
   - Seed window (µm) — about one cell across; it decides what counts as one object.
   - Foreground threshold — raise it if background is coming through as cells.
6. **Preview before you commit** — This runs the real compute over just the region the viewer is showing.
   - Seconds instead of minutes — the way to judge the diameter and channels.
   - Open the image in the viewer first; the preview follows what it shows.
7. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
8. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
9. **Check the QC first** — Same plots as any segmentation — too few cells, implausible sizes, edge artefacts.
   - Compare it against a cellpose run on the same image if you have one.
10. **Open it in the viewer** — The ↗ opens the image itself — the overlay is a separate switch.
11. **Open the Viewer panel** — This panel drives the viewer — overlays, contrast, 3D, recording.
12. **Switch the mask on** — Nothing is drawn on the image until you toggle the mask for that segmentation.
   - One row per segmentation, each with its own switches.
   - The choice is remembered, so it comes back next time you open the image.
13. **Now judge the mask** — With it on screen, this is what to look for.
   - Do the labels stay on the same cell as it moves?
   - Is a moving cell one object, or does it break up between frames?
14. **What you now have** — Labels and measures on a movie cellpose could not read — track them next.
   - Tracking is the point of segmenting a movie; gating works on these too.

title: Create and gate populations
summary: Draw gates on two measures at a time to carve your cells into named populations.
text:
# Create and gate populations

Draw gates on two measures at a time to carve your cells into named populations.

Needs: an open project; a segmented image.

1. **Gate** — Gating is FlowJo-style: pick two measures, draw round the cells you want, name them.
2. **One image at a time** — Gating works on a single image — pick one and its cells load below.
   - Gates can be copied to the rest of the set once you are happy with them.
3. **Which segmentation** — You gate on the measures of one label set — pick it here if you have several.
4. Add a plot — each one is a pair of measures you can draw on.
5. **Choose the two measures** — X and Y take any channel intensity or shape measure the segmentation carried.
   - The transform beside each axis is usually what makes a blob resolve into groups.
   - "pop" is the population you are looking at — new gates land under it.
6. **Pick a shape** — Choose a gate shape, then draw on the plot — drag for a rectangle, click to place polygon points.
   - Hold Shift to adjust a gate you already drew.
7. **Name it** — A population is just a named gate — the name is how everything downstream refers to it.
   - Names are case-insensitively unique across the whole tree, not just among siblings.
   - A leading underscore is reserved for tracked / clustering populations.
8. The population manager shows the tree you are building.
9. **Gates nest** — Each population shows its cell count and its share of its parent.
   - Click one to plot it, then draw inside it to subset further.
   - That nesting is the gating strategy — CD3+ → CD4+ → activated.
10. **Populations are live** — Gates are stored as definitions, not as a frozen list of cells.
   - Re-segment and your gates still apply.
   - Populations show up in the viewer, in plots, and as a tracking input.

title: Track cells
summary: Link segmented cells across frames into tracks, with speed and direction for free.
text:
# Track cells

Link segmented cells across frames into tracks, with speed and direction for free.

Needs: an open project; a time series (more than one frame); a segmented image.
Runs: `tracking.bayesian_track_measures`.

1. **Track** — Tracking links labels across frames — so segment every timepoint before you come here.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Each image needs a segmentation covering all of its frames.
   - It must be a MEASURED segmentation — the Segment guide's function does both.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Bayesian track + measures" from the dropdown.
   - Plain "Bayesian tracking" links cells but computes no per-track measures.
   - This one measures too — speed, displacement, angle — which is what you gate and cluster on.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Segmentation — which label set to track; a gated population narrows it.
   - Max search radius (µm) — the furthest a cell may move between frames (~20 for T cells).
   - Allowed gaps and minimum timepoints — how forgiving linking is, and what counts as a real track.
   - Motion dimensions — 2D or 3D for the measures; it detects and recommends one.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **Open it in the viewer** — The ↗ opens the image itself — the overlay is a separate switch.
9. **Open the Viewer panel** — This panel drives the viewer — overlays, contrast, 3D, recording.
10. **Switch the tracks on** — Nothing is drawn on the image until you toggle the tracks for that segmentation.
   - One row per segmentation, each with its own switches.
   - The choice is remembered, so it comes back next time you open the image.
11. **Now judge the tracks** — With it on screen, this is what to look for.
   - Do the trails follow single cells, or jump between neighbours?
   - Jumping usually means the search radius is too generous.
12. **Gate on track properties** — This is the gating canvas in track mode — one point per track, not per cell.
   - Gate on speed, displacement and the other per-track aggregates.
   - Select exactly one image to use it.
13. **What you now have** — Tracks are in, and measured — speed, displacement and angle came with them.
   - Every cell has a track_id and a position at each timepoint.
   - Behaviour → HMM fits states to those measures; Cluster tracks groups on both.

title: Cluster cells into phenotypes
summary: Group cells by their whole measure profile instead of gating two channels at a time.
text:
# Cluster cells into phenotypes

Group cells by their whole measure profile instead of gating two channels at a time.

Needs: an open project; a segmented image.
Runs: `clustPops.cluster`.

1. **Cluster cells** — Clustering finds cell types from all measures at once — the unsupervised counterpart to gating.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Select every image you want clustered TOGETHER — the run pools across them.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Cluster cells" from the dropdown.
   - Clustering CELLS — the track counterpart is its own page, and needs tracking first.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Populations — which cells to cluster; every selection is clustered jointly.
   - Cluster on — the feature columns, usually the channel intensities.
   - Resolution — the Leiden resolution; higher gives more, smaller clusters.
   - Calculate UMAP — leave on, it is what the embedding plot draws.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **UMAP plus heatmap** — The UMAP shows how clusters separate; the heatmap says what each one actually expresses.
   - The heatmap is what turns "cluster 4" into "CD4 T cell".
   - Read it before naming anything — it says what each cluster expresses.
9. **Clusters are numbers, not populations yet** — Open the population manager — this is where numbered clusters become named groups.
10. **Add a population** — There is no gate to draw here — you create the population first, then fill it.
   - Name it for what it is: "patrolling", "CD4 T cell".
11. **Tick clusters into it** — Each chip is one cluster — click to put it in this population.
   - A cluster belongs to at most one population; ticking it elsewhere moves it.
   - The heatmap is how you decide which clusters belong together.
12. **Now it behaves like any population** — Your phenotype populations are usable everywhere a gated one is.
   - Plot them on the analysis board, show them in the viewer, use them as an input.
   - Populations are per clustering run — they follow that run's suffix.

title: Cluster tracks into behaviours
summary: Group whole tracks by how they move, rather than grouping cells by what they express.
text:
# Cluster tracks into behaviours

Group whole tracks by how they move, rather than grouping cells by what they express.

Needs: an open project; a tracked image.
Runs: `clustTracks.cluster`.

1. **Cluster tracks** — One row per track instead of per cell — so this needs tracking, not just segmentation.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Select every image to cluster TOGETHER — the run pools across them.
   - Needs measured tracks — the Track guide's function does both.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Cluster tracks" from the dropdown.
   - Cell measures are aggregated per track for you; HMM states become per-track frequencies.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Track populations — which tracks to cluster; every selection is clustered jointly.
   - Cluster on — whole-track measures plus the HMM state and transitions columns (run HMM first).
   - Minimum track length — drop tracks too short to characterise.
   - Resolution — the Leiden resolution; higher gives more, smaller clusters.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **Clusters of movement** — The UMAP separates behaviours; the heatmap says which measures define each one.
   - This answers "how many kinds of movement are in here", without naming them first.
   - With the HMM states and transitions in, it separates behaviours track averages blur.
9. **Clusters are numbers, not populations yet** — Open the population manager — this is where numbered clusters become named groups.
10. **Add a population** — There is no gate to draw here — you create the population first, then fill it.
   - Name it for what it is: "patrolling", "CD4 T cell".
11. **Tick clusters into it** — Each chip is one cluster — click to put it in this population.
   - A cluster belongs to at most one population; ticking it elsewhere moves it.
   - The heatmap is how you decide which clusters belong together.
12. **Now it behaves like any population** — Your behaviour populations are usable everywhere a gated one is.
   - Plot them on the analysis board, show them in the viewer, use them as an input.
   - Populations are per clustering run — they follow that run's suffix.

title: Cluster spatial regions
summary: Group spatial neighbourhoods — what surrounds each cell — into named regions you can plot and gate.
text:
# Cluster spatial regions

Group spatial neighbourhoods — what surrounds each cell — into named regions you can plot and gate.

Needs: an open project; a segmented image.
Runs: `clustRegions.cluster`.

1. **Cluster regions** — Region clustering groups NEIGHBOURHOODS ("what surrounds each cell"), not the cells themselves.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Select every image you want clustered TOGETHER — the composition vectors pool across them.

   - Neighbour graph — the graph a Spatial run produced; pick one to cluster over.
   - Population basis — the populations whose mix defines each neighbourhood's composition vector.
   - Suffix — output name for this run; you pick it again when reading the regions downstream.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **Read the regions** — UMAP shows how the neighbourhoods separate; the heatmap says what each region is composed of.
   - Bright rows on the heatmap = the populations that define that region.
   - Rename a region once its composition is clear — "T-cell rich", "vessel edge".
9. **Clusters are numbers, not populations yet** — Open the population manager — this is where numbered clusters become named groups.
10. **Add a population** — There is no gate to draw here — you create the population first, then fill it.
   - Name it for what it is: "patrolling", "CD4 T cell".
11. **Tick clusters into it** — Each chip is one cluster — click to put it in this population.
   - A cluster belongs to at most one population; ticking it elsewhere moves it.
   - The heatmap is how you decide which clusters belong together.
12. **Now it behaves like any population** — Your region populations are usable everywhere a gated one is.
   - Plot them on the analysis board, show them in the viewer, use them as an input.
   - Populations are per clustering run — they follow that run's suffix.

title: Correct a mask or a track
summary: The hand-tools for fixing what an automated run got wrong — merge, split, redraw, delete.
text:
# Correct a mask or a track

The hand-tools for fixing what an automated run got wrong — merge, split, redraw, delete.

Needs: an open project; a segmented image.

1. **The correction cockpit** — When segmentation gets a cell wrong, fix it here — a floating panel that sits over the viewer so you keep looking at the image.
2. **Pick a mode** — Tracks / Labels / Review — each drives its own queue and toolbar.
   - Review pages over the picked labels one at a time.
3. **Toolbar for this mode** — Each verb QUEUES an edit — nothing is applied until you press Apply below.
   - Undo removes the last queued edit; Clear drops all of them.
4. **What is picked** — Chips show the tracks or labels the toolbar acts on — click a chip to drop it.
   - No strip = nothing picked yet; the summary line below still names the state.
5. **Apply — it becomes a new version** — Applying writes a new label-set version — the original run is preserved.
   - Downstream tasks read the ACTIVE version, like everywhere else.

title: Classify behaviour states
summary: Fit an HMM to track movement so each cell gets an arrested / directed / meandering state.
text:
# Classify behaviour states

Fit an HMM to track movement so each cell gets an arrested / directed / meandering state.

Needs: an open project; a tracked image.
Runs: `behaviour.hmm`.

1. **Behaviour** — A Gaussian HMM turns raw track movement into a small set of named behaviour states.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Only tracked images qualify — the states are fitted to track measures.
   - The tracking must have MEASURED — the Track guide's function does both.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "HMM (states + transitions)" from the dropdown.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Number of states — 3 is the usual starting point (arrested / meandering / directed).
   - Which track measures to fit on — speed and angle are the standard pair.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **Read the states off the plots** — The panel shows what each fitted state actually looks like, so you can name them.
   - A state is only meaningful once you have seen its speed profile.
   - Fit landed oddly? Change the number of states and re-run.
9. **Colour tracks by state** — The Viewer panel can colour tracks by the new state column.
   - That is the quickest sanity check that the states mean something.

title: Score spatial interactions
summary: Who is near whom, and how often — the interaction matrix and per-image contact stats.
text:
# Score spatial interactions

Who is near whom, and how often — the interaction matrix and per-image contact stats.

Needs: an open project; a segmented image.
Runs: `spatialAnalysis.neighbourStats`.

1. **Spatial** — Reads relationships between populations on the image — who is near whom, and how often.
2. Check the active set is the one you mean — functions only see this set.
3. **Tick the images to run on** — Selection is per page, and it is remembered when you navigate away.
   - Tick as many as you like — one task is queued per image.
4. **Choose the function** — Pick "Interaction matrix" from the dropdown.
   - Neighbour graph runs first — this task LOADS it, does not build it.
   - Interaction matrix, Aggregates and Contacts all live in this dropdown; this guide teaches the matrix.
5. **Set the parameters** — These are the settings worth getting right before you run.
   - Neighbour graph — the graph a Neighbour-graph run produced; pick the one you want scored.
   - Population basis — the pairs to score interactions between; at least two.
   - Name — output name for this run; a later plot picks it up by this name.
6. Happy with the preview? Run it — one task per selected image.
7. **Watch it here** — Every run appears in this rail with its live log, progress and a cancel button.
   - You can leave the page — runs are server-side, not tab-side.
   - Click a row to read its log.
8. **Read the matrix** — Log-odds heatmap: bright cells co-locate more than chance; dark ones avoid.
   - The permutation test tells you if a pattern is a real signal or the same cell types rearranged.
   - Contacts and aggregates plot the same underlying graph in different shapes — worth a look next.

title: Build plots
summary: Lay out summary plots across images on a board, then export the figure and its data.
text:
# Build plots

Lay out summary plots across images on a board, then export the figure and its data.

Needs: an open project; a segmented image.

1. **Analysis board** — A board is a grid of plot slots you fill, arrange, and export as one figure.
2. **Pick what to plot across** — Tick the images the board should summarise — plots pool across your selection.
   - Attributes (treatment, mouse) are what you will group by later.
3. **Fill a slot** — Each empty slot offers every plot this page has — summary, interactive, clustering.
   - A plot whose run has not happened yet renders empty rather than being hidden.
   - The clustering ones DO hide until a run of that kind exists.
4. **Choose the populations** — The rail on the right picks which populations the active plot draws.
   - This page is READ-ONLY — you pick populations here, you do not edit them.
   - To change a gate, go back to the Gate page.
5. **Plot options** — The gear holds how the active plot is drawn — and how it groups your images.
   - Compare by an attribute to split the plot by treatment or genotype.
   - Options are saved with the board.
6. **Boards are cheap** — One board per question — they are tabs, they autosave, and they can be duplicated.
7. **Export** — One control for the figure and the numbers behind it.
   - SVG is true vector — editable in Illustrator or Inkscape.
   - CSV gives you the tidy data, so a figure is never unreproducible.

title: Record a movie
summary: Record what the viewer is showing as an mp4, then repeat the same look across a whole set.
text:
# Record a movie

Record what the viewer is showing as an mp4, then repeat the same look across a whole set.

Needs: an open project; a time series (more than one frame).

1. **Set the shot up first** — A recording captures exactly what the viewer is showing — so get the view right before you record.
   - Open the image with the ↗ beside it.
   - Channels, contrast, masks, tracks, populations: all of it is recorded as shown.
2. **Open the Viewer panel** — The overlay switches and the recorder both live here.
3. **The Movie block** — The gear holds fps, output size, filename, timestamp, scale bar and the title card.
   - Trim the time range here if you only want part of the timelapse.
   - Pick two versions to record them side by side instead.
4. **Record** — The render runs as a task, so progress and Cancel are in the task list.
   - The mp4 lands in the project's movies/ folder.
   - The renderer processes one frame at a time — leave it alone while it sweeps.
5. **Where they land** — Every movie from any of the three routes shows up on this page, with a player.
6. **Now do it for the whole set** — Batch movies applies one config to every image you select, instead of one at a time.
   - This is the point of getting the single one right first.
7. **Pick the images** — Tick every image you want a movie of — one mp4 comes out per image.
8. **Generate** — Configure channels, size and the title card in the panel, then record the lot.
   - The config is remembered per set, so the next batch starts where you left off.
   - Each movie is its own task — watch them in the list below.
9. **Two more things worth knowing** — Movies are rendered frame by frame, so they cost real time on long timelapses.
   - Everything lands in movies/ and is playable on the Movies page.
   - Want a camera move instead of a straight sweep? See the "Build an animation" guide.

title: Build an animation
summary: Capture viewer views as keyframes and tween between them — a camera move, not a time sweep.
text:
# Build an animation

Capture viewer views as keyframes and tween between them — a camera move, not a time sweep.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing.

1. **Animation** — A recording sweeps time with one fixed look; an animation moves between looks you choose.
   - A keyframe holds the camera, the channels, the populations and the timepoint.
   - So it can pan, fade a channel in and travel through time at once.
2. **One image at a time** — A timeline belongs to a single image — pick one and its keyframes appear below.
3. **Open it in the viewer** — Every capture reads the live viewer, so the viewer has to be showing the image.
   - This button disappears once it is open.
4. **Set the view up, then capture** — Arrange it in the viewer exactly as you want the shot to start — then take the keyframe.
   - Camera angle, zoom, channels, contrast, overlays, timepoint: all recorded.
   - This first one is your base look.
5. **The timeline** — Columns are keyframes; rows are the channels, populations and camera read from each one.
   - The slider under a column is how many seconds it tweens FROM the previous one.
   - Drag columns to reorder; an "edited" badge means it differs from what was captured.
6. **Add the next one** — Two ways: duplicate the last keyframe and vary it in the rows, or re-capture from the viewer.
   - Add keyframe — duplicates, for a small change you make in the timeline.
   - Update selected — replaces a keyframe with the current viewer view.
7. **Render** — Needs two keyframes at least — there is nothing to tween between with one.
   - fps, output size and the title card are the same controls as the other two routes.
   - It renders as a task; progress is in the list below.
8. **Where it lands** — Animations join the recordings and batch movies on the Movies page.
   - Keyframes are saved with the project, so you can come back and adjust.

title: Create a notebook
summary: Open a Pluto notebook wired to your project for analysis the built-in plots do not cover.
text:
# Create a notebook

Open a Pluto notebook wired to your project for analysis the built-in plots do not cover.

Needs: an open project.

1. **Notebooks** — Notebooks are the escape hatch: reactive Julia on your project data, no export needed.
2. **Start the server** — Pluto runs as its own server — start it once per session.
   - The first launch precompiles and can take a minute.
3. **Add a notebook** — Name it and add it — you get a notebook with the whole stack already loaded.
   - Cecelia and the plotting packages are imported and configured for you.
   - Fill in the project and image uid in the template's first cell and go.
   - Shipped examples are listed below, read-only — duplicate one to edit it.
4. **The registry** — Every notebook in the project, with a snapshot history you can roll back to.
   - The ↗ button opens one in Pluto, in a new tab.
   - Snapshot before a big edit — that is the provenance trail.
5. **Fast plots** — The first plot compiles from scratch unless you build the fast-plot cache.
   - It is optional — notebooks work without it, just slow on the first plot.
   - The build takes ~10 min in the background.
6. **One thing to know** — Pluto is reactive: changing a cell re-runs everything that depends on it.
   - So there is no stale-state confusion, but a slow cell re-runs more often.
   - Ask Claude to draft a notebook for you — it can create one in this registry.

title: Use the blackboard
summary: Shared markdown between you and the assist — where a conclusion becomes durable, not chat scrollback.
text:
# Use the blackboard

Shared markdown between you and the assist — where a conclusion becomes durable, not chat scrollback.

Needs: an open project.

1. **Blackboard** — One markdown surface per project — every Kiwi turn about this project lands here too.
   - Reach it from the sidebar; the list opens straight away.
2. **Start an entry** — One entry per thought you are chasing — captures land under it as they arrive from the viewer or Kiwi.
   - Entries are per project — open a project first.
3. **The entry list** — Sort by any column; the two chip rows above filter by status and outcome.
   - The project profile row stays pinned to the top.
4. **Edit and version** — Edit takes a snapshot before saving — every revision is kept and previewable from the version dropdown.
   - Restore v3 with a click if v4 went sideways.
5. **Tag outcome** — Good or Bad plus a note when the thread is settled — what carries into the next project.
   - The note is required; it is what a future session actually needs to know.
6. **Send to Kiwi** — Feed this entry (or a specific version) into a Kiwi turn — appears as context alongside your prompt.
   - Ships the version you are viewing.

title: Assist with Kiwi
summary: The assistant cockpit — pairing status, chat handoff, and sharing what is on screen.
text:
# Assist with Kiwi

The assistant cockpit — pairing status, chat handoff, and sharing what is on screen.

Needs: an open project.

1. **The lab log** — A per-project, append-only record — Cecelia adds a digest when a run finishes, you and Kiwi append notes.
   - Floating panel, reachable from any page.
2. **Kiwi is the assist cockpit** — Everything Claude-adjacent lives in this panel — pairing, chat starter, and the buttons that share what is on screen.
   - On-demand only; nothing happens until you ask.
3. **Pairing status** — The chip shows whether a claude-code session on this machine is paired — the refresh button probes the socket.
   - Unpaired Kiwi still holds state; shared frames just fall back to the clipboard.
4. **Copy a chat starter** — Copies a one-line opener naming this project — paste it into the paired session to start a Kiwi conversation about it.
5. **Ship what you are looking at** — Two targets: the viewer frame or a canvas plot — both land in the same capture envelope.
   - Falls back to the clipboard if nothing is paired.
6. **What Kiwi can see and do** — This ? explains Ask vs Chat, captures, chains, blackboard, limits — read once.
   - Also reports whether the assist is actually set up.

title: Run a pipeline over a whole set
summary: Wire your steps into a chain once, then run the lot across every image in a set.
text:
# Run a pipeline over a whole set

Wire your steps into a chain once, then run the lot across every image in a set.

Needs: an open project; an image that finished importing.

1. **Whiteboard** — A chain is your pipeline drawn as a graph — correct, segment, track, cluster, in order.
   - Build it once and every new image goes through the same steps.
2. **Chains are named templates** — Make one per pipeline you use — they are saved with the project.
3. **Drag in the steps** — Every function from every module page is here — drag one onto the canvas.
   - Connect nodes to set the order.
   - A node only runs if it is reachable from the start node.
4. **Pick the images** — Choose the set and tick the images to push through the chain.
   - Excluded images are greyed out and cannot be selected.
5. Run it — each image walks the whole graph, and the pools cap what runs at once.
6. **Watch it live** — The Live tab shows the graph filling in per image, with QC as it lands.
   - A failure skips only what depends on it — other images and parallel branches carry on.
   - You can resume a run from a chosen node rather than starting over.
7. **This is how you scale** — Everything the module pages do one image at a time, a chain does for a cohort unattended.
